View in browser             Sponsored by       Dawn Gilbertson   My Airline Lost and Found Saga With a Happy but Head-Scratching Ending   Plus, JD Power’s airport rankings and an update on Europe’s messy new passport control system   Happy Friday from the Sonoran Desert, where I think we’re finally over daily triple-digit temperatures. 

   In travel news this week, airlines said travel demand remains strong despite a host of economic pressures. You know what that means: Fares aren’t going down anytime soon. I would lock in those holiday flights now, especially if your travel plans aren’t flexible or you are loyal to one airline. 

   JD Power released its annual North America Airport Satisfaction Study and the big winners in each size category were Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport, Tampa International Airport and Charleston International Airport. See how your airport fared and let me know if you agree with the results. 

   The new passport control system in the EU remains a mixed bag, with reports this week that nine countries have told the government they aren’t going to fully implement it due to continuing long lines and other issues. One reader returning to California from Europe this week said he missed his connecting flight in Frankfurt despite a 75-minute cushion between flights. His layover recommendation: at least two hours. 

   American Express opened its latest Centurion lounge at Amsterdam’s Schiphol airport. It is located between Concourses E and F. 

   Celebrity Cruises this week reached a major construction milestone on its first river ship, Celebrity Compass. The first river cruise is still nearly a year away, though. 

   And Frontier Airlines plans to launch flights to Colombia in December, with nonstop service between Orlando and Medellín, Bogotá and Cartagena. 

       My bizarre airport lost and found story     My mini wallet was somewhere at Newark airport. MICHAEL NAGLE/BLOOMBERG NEWS   I tend to avoid airports on my day off since I traverse them nonstop for this job. So why did I spend four hours and $41 on public transit to and from Newark last Saturday? To retrieve a lost Lululemon credit card holder. 

   Airline lost and found can be a black hole , as anyone who has left something in a seat back pocket, overhead bin, gate or anywhere at the airport really, knows too well.

   I share this not to publicly flog myself for another travel faux pas but to give you hope or prompt you to broaden your search.

   Let’s call this case a head-scratcher. I left my mini wallet in the seat back pocket, seat or maybe floor of a United Airlines flight from Chicago to Newark. (I never take my wallet out on the plane but needed to use a new card to buy another plane ticket.)

   I realized it was gone about halfway through my Lyft ride to Manhattan and filed a claim with United via the Chargerback service they use as soon as I got to my hotel. (I still had my corporate card so checking in and dining out wasn’t an issue.)

   My ticket was in first class where passengers get priority status for everything, so I figured I might get it back quickly.

   But I heard nothing besides a form letter that they were still looking. Three days later, my phone rang early in the morning. The customer service agent said my wallet was in American’s baggage claim office. I asked him twice if he meant United!

   He didn’t know where or when it was found except that it was found in a Newark gate area, where I spent no time after landing. He brought it to the American baggage services office and called after tracking me down, probably by the AA frequent flier number on my new AA credit card I pulled out on the plane. (I keep my IDs separate and have an AirTag in my purse but not a separate one in the wallet.)

   A United spokesman told me flight attendants and cleaning crews are instructed to turn any items over to customer service. In terminals where multiple airlines operate, as in Newark’s new Terminal A, he says it’s feasible that whoever found it handed it over to the nearest airline employee.

   Whatever path it took, I was thrilled to have it back. I headed to Newark the long way because you can’t expense stupidity.

   Do you have any tales of lost items that took a circuitous path back to you? Share them at dawn.gilbertson@wsj.com or by replying to this email.

On most Mint flights.   Learn More  >       One Good Tip 🎯   This one comes from readers responding to my column on seat downgrades this week. When booking a seat in first class or business class, try to avoid the last couple of rows in case there’s a last-minute switch to a smaller plane with fewer premium seats. This isn’t foolproof, of course, because many factors including loyalty status go into deciding who gets bumped out of a seat. But it can’t hurt.

       Travel Math 🧮   50%   The portion of American Airlines’ revenue coming from 30% of its seats, those premium seats that are all the rage, CEO Robert Isom said this week.

       And We Quote 💬   “The longer this business sees good times where we have tons of pilot hirings, the more people forget the past.” 

   — Southwest pilot and pilot podcast host Max Palmer, on wealthy pilots who splurge on boats, cars and planes, forgetting about past layoffs and industry crises. 

       You Have Thoughts 🤔   …on   tardy airport shuttles :

   • “You were lucky. At least the Hyatt Regency shuttle told you not to board. When the Doubletree shuttle showed up at Newark airport for a five-minute trip to the hotel and an overnight stay for an early morning flight, we got on. It dropped us 25 minutes later at the wrong Doubletree. The address of the hotel was covered by the door, and the driver didn’t bother to ask, ‘Which Doubletree are you going to?’ or to tell people he was going to a downtown Doubletree, not the airport Doubletree. Always check which hotel.” — Peter Zollman, Florida  

   (Responses have been condensed and edited.) 

       Cheers and Jeers 🤷   Cheers to hotels that will deliver a professional-grade steamer to your room. I’m perfectly fine with one of those hand-held devices but loved the standing unit at the Hyatt Centric Times Square last week.

   Jeers to no ride-share service at Terminal 5 at Chicago O’Hare. You have to hop a shuttle to another terminal or wait in an interminable taxi line. I opted for the airport hotel shuttle.

One Good Tip 🎯

 

This one comes from readers responding to my column on seat downgrades this week. When booking a seat in first class or business class, try to avoid the last couple of rows in case there’s a last-minute switch to a smaller plane with fewer premium seats. This isn’t foolproof, of course, because many factors including loyalty status go into deciding who gets bumped out of a seat. But it can’t hurt.

The portion of American Airlines’ revenue coming from 30% of its seats, those premium seats that are all the rage, CEO Robert Isom said this week.
